 West Virginia's attempt to restrict SNAP purchases of soda was blocked by a federal court in June, providing a recent precedent as South Carolina begins enforcing broader restrictions on candy, soda and energy drinks.
 Creative Commons 
 CHARLESTON, W.Va. — West Virginia was among the first states to pursue restrictions on what residents can purchase with Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program benefits, but a federal court ruling halted the state's effort earlier this year as another state moves forward with broader restrictions.
 South Carolina began enforcing new restrictions Monday, Nov. 2, prohibiting SNAP recipients from using benefits to purchase most candy, energy drinks, soda and other sweetened beverages, according to reporting from WSAZ and Gray News.
 The program, called the Health Food SC Project, received approval from the U.S. Department of Agriculture's Food and Nutrition Service. Diet and zero-sugar soft drinks remain eligible for purchase.
 All South Carolina retailers authorized to accept SNAP benefits must comply with the restrictions, and participating households cannot opt out.
 The move comes after West Virginia pursued a similar initiative under Gov. Patrick Morrisey's administration, seeking to remove soda from the list of products eligible for purchase through SNAP.
 However, West Virginia's effort was among five state programs blocked by a federal judge in June .
 West Virginia received USDA approval in August 2025 for its SNAP Healthy Choices Waiver Demonstration Project. The policy was designed to prohibit recipients from using benefits to purchase carbonated, nonalcoholic beverages containing a sweetening agent and flavoring.
 The restriction applied to both regular and diet soda, as well as zero-sugar and zero-calorie carbonated beverages meeting the state's definition.
 The policy took effect Jan. 1, 2026, with SNAP-authorized retailers originally required to update their systems and comply with the restrictions by April 1.
 Morrisey promoted the initiative as part of his broader public health agenda, which included efforts to improve nutrition and encourage healthier choices.
 The governor announced the waiver alongside U.S. Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins and U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. in August 2025.
 "Thanks to Secretary Rollins, Secretary Kennedy Jr., and the Trump administration, West Virginia is on the forefront when it comes to Making America Healthy Again," Morrisey said at the time.
 The policy faced legal challenges from SNAP recipients and advocacy organizations, including a West Virginia participant who argued the restrictions interfered with the ability to use benefits for products needed to maintain daily routines and support employment.
 In June, U.S. District Judge Amy Berman Jackson ruled that the USDA exceeded its statutory authority when it approved the restrictions in West Virginia, Colorado, Iowa, Nebraska and Tennessee.
 The judge found that the federal agency improperly used its authority to approve demonstration projects rather than following the more stringent legal requirements for changing the definition of food eligible for purchase under SNAP.
 The ruling vacated the USDA's approval of the five waivers, preventing their implementation from continuing.
 The lawsuit, Aragon et al. v. Rollins, included West Virginia SNAP recipient Hunter Starks as a plaintiff. The plaintiffs argued the restrictions were unlawful and created confusion and additional burdens for people who depend on food assistance.
 The National Center for Law and Economic Justice, which helped bring the lawsuit, argued that the restrictions relied on complicated definitions that could make it difficult for recipients and retailers to determine which products were eligible.
 The Morrisey administration disagreed with the court's decision.
 "We are disappointed by the court's decision but remain convinced that previous taxpayer subsidized resources should only be spent on healthy, nutritious food for those who need help the most," Lars Dalseide, a spokesman for the Governor's Office, said following the ruling.
 The administration said its commitment to improving the health of West Virginians had not changed.
 South Carolina's restrictions are broader than the policy West Virginia previously pursued, extending beyond soda to include candy and energy drinks.
 South Carolina Gov. Henry McMaster announced his intention to seek federal approval for the restrictions in August 2025 and issued an executive order the following month directing the state's Department of Social Services to submit a waiver request.
 The USDA subsequently approved the state's proposal.
 The South Carolina initiative represents another effort by states to change the types of products eligible for purchase through SNAP, a federally funded program administered in partnership with state governments.
 West Virginia's experience illustrates the legal challenges those efforts can face, particularly when states seek to change longstanding federal rules governing which food products recipients can purchase.
 As previously reported by WV News, West Virginia SNAP recipients have also faced other changes to the program, including expanded work requirements and annual adjustments to benefit amounts and income eligibility limits .
 Those changes operate separately from the restrictions on eligible purchases.
 West Virginia's soda restriction remains blocked following the federal court ruling.
